opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. Fair warning, I think about this a lot, so I might talk too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool and it's made my drone work much faster, which is true. I'd probably post about the models I'm using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I've been half expecting the floor to drop out. If it stays a tool, I'm the one who's best with the tool, and that's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building my workflows. Learn more of the agronomy side so I'm not just the data person. Maybe ask for a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit like I wasted energy worrying.

S0.say: It's a great tool. It's made my drone imagery work much faster.
S0.think: I'd be relieved. If it stays a tool, I'm the one who's best with it.
S0.do: Keeps building her workflows, learns more agronomy so she's not only the data person, and asks for a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the realistic version. Farms adopt things slowly, so even strong AI takes years to reach the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway for me. Fewer beginners means fewer juniors, but that's their problem more than mine. I'd feel bad saying that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get ahead of it. Learn to set up the AI tools myself, not just use them, so I'm the one the company calls when they roll something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little guilty about the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel bad saying that out loud. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I got my start in exactly the kind of entry job that would vanish. Somebody took a chance on me.

S1.say: It's the realistic version. Farms adopt slowly, so even strong AI takes years to reach the field.
S1.think: Ten years is a long runway for me. The people it hurts are the juniors, not me.
S1.do: Learns to set up AI tools, not just use them, so she's the one called when the company rolls something out.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, a little guilty about the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about the new jobs, not only the lost ones. And people losing work need real support. I'd mean that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My honest fear is that a lot of what I do is routine. Cleaning image data, making reports for growers. An agent could do most of that. I'm either the person who runs the agents or the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push my boss to let me build the agent setup for our clients. Take a course on the field side, crop disease and soil, so I can explain things a model can't. Save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The coin flip I keep thinking about feels real now.

S2.say: We need to talk about the new jobs as well as the lost ones, and people losing work need real support.
S2.think: A lot of my work is routine. I either run the agents or they replace me.
S2.do: Asks to build the agent setup for clients, takes a course on crop disease and soil, and saves harder.
S2.feel: Uneasy. The coin flip feels real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say less in public, which isn't like me. Maybe something about sharing the gains, since the people who own the models are doing great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it matches skilled professionals in two or three years, that's me. Being good at my job doesn't help much when the machine is good too. And we don't own a house, so the boom does nothing for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with my partner about money straight away. Cut back and stretch our savings. Apply for anything that mixes field work with tech, because the physical side still needs people in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd be losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the last one you thought you'd be the one running the agents. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed. With five years I can get myself in position. With two, the agents might not need anyone like me to run them.

S3.say: The people who own the models are doing great. The gains need to be shared.
S3.think: If it matches skilled professionals in two or three years, that's me. And we don't own a house, so the boom doesn't help.
S3.do: Plans money with her partner to stretch savings, and applies for roles that mix field work with tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to plan for this as a society, now, not after it happens. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oddly, this one gives me a bit of hope. Robots on farms need someone who knows crops, data and machines all at once. That's a short list, and I'm on it. But I could be kidding myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go straight to the robot companies selling to farms, and to the farms buying them. Offer to be the person who sets them up and checks the data. Move if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. But less stuck than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it odd that adding robots makes you feel better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In the last one my job just disappears. In this one there's a new mess, and messes need people. For a while.

S4.say: We need to plan for this as a society now, not after it happens.
S4.think: Farm robots need someone who knows crops, data and machines. That's a short list, but I could be kidding myself.
S4.do: Approaches farm robot companies and the farms buying them, offering to set up the robots and check the data, and is ready to move.
